In most areas and where properly operated and managed, ORV do limited damage to the human environment, physical resources, flora, fauna, and cultural resources. The vehicles can also provide safe and convenient transportation to portions of the public lands not otherwise accessible to the benefits of society for official as well as pleasure use.
Available information indicates that there are opposing points of view concerning the use of ORV as a means of strengthening family ties. These views range from one extreme to the other, depending upon the interests of the particular individuals. Some information discloses that ORV use creates family stresses and strains and separates the family as a unit. Other information in ORV user-oriented magazines and letters from ORV enthusiasts indicates that ORV activities are participated in as a family sport and keep the family together in regards to other related recreational activities.
Information available in ORV trade journals and ORV industry reports indicates that in some snowbelt states and other areas of the U.S. where there is widespread ORV use, there have been considerable economic benefits from sales of goods and services related to ORV use.
In some areas and where improperly or indiscriminately used, ORV can cause substantial irreversible and irretrievable harm to man and his natural environment.
Even when properly operated, the impact may be great and, in many instances, irretrievable on individually-designated areas. Most difficult of assessment and management will be determination of use levels which will be compatible with the resource base and yet provide the recreation or benefits sought by ORV user groups. Data regarding these concerns is limited and individual bureaus (coordinated by the Assistant Secretary—Program Development and Budget) will monitor the effects of ORV use on lands under their jurisdiction to assist in closing this information gap.
A) Physical Impacts:
Practically no area of the public lands is free from potential damage by ORV. This fact alone necessitates action to protect fragile and susceptible land forms; desert, tundra, swamp, marsh, sand dunes, ice and snow fields, and steep terrain. The prohibition of ORV from a public land area would negate any impacts from those sources upon the areas' soils, water, air, and visual qualities.
Soils in many areas of the public lands are susceptible to erosion, compaction, or displacement. In highly erodible soils, soil movement may increase and the hydrological functioning of the soil may be impaired. Soil impaction affects ecological productivity and hydrological functioning.
